When you run a proprietary program (like Adobe Photoshop or a closed-source game) on your PC, you get a compiled binary of machine code. The high-level logic is stripped out, variables are obfuscated, and the EULA legally forbids you from decompiling, reverse-engineering, or modifying the binary.

So you can inspect the exact mathematical state of the model at any arbitrary moment during inference -- in other words, you can study open models.  You can fine-tune or quantize them -- in other words, you can improve them quite significantly!  And much much more.

text:
An underrated quality of parser combinators is that they're often written in continuation passing style (monadic style is a simple generalisation of this). So, you get "incremental" parsing for free (as "what to do next" is trivially available). So, many of these parsers work well on streams (e.g. TCP sockets) without manually maintaining a state machine - as you may do in C. Further to this, such a state machine is derivable by defunctionalising the parser combinator code. Of course, you get the same benefit if you have decent coroutine support, but it's nice to see techniques that work around not having runtime/language support for such niceties.

There's another, more obscure, technique in the functional programming world called [iteratees](https://okmij.org/ftp/Haskell/Iteratee/index.html) which are quite neat and (as done in related article) linked to "online parser combinators".
